Chapter Two: How We Know What’s True—Evidence, Testing, and the Power of Science.
Picture this: you and a few friends are standing at the edge of a quiet forest, and suddenly, a strange sound echoes through the trees. One friend swears it’s a spirit. Another shrugs and says it’s just the wind, while someone else is sure it’s an animal. Everyone’s got a story, a hunch, or maybe a memory that backs up what they believe. But here’s the real question—how can anyone be sure?
That’s the challenge we all face: telling the difference between what’s real, and what’s just imagined. For most of history, people leaned on stories, trusted authority, or stuck with tradition to make sense of the world. And while those ways can feel reassuring, they often give us wildly different answers to the same mystery. If everyone’s story leads somewhere else, how do we know what’s actually true?
The answer? It’s a whole new approach—one that doesn’t depend on who’s telling the tale, but on what can be seen, tested, and repeated. That’s the foundation of science. Instead of grabbing onto the first explanation that comes along, science says: where’s the evidence? It’s not enough to believe something just because someone said so. The real question becomes, “What can we actually see, measure, or test?”
So, let’s go back to that group of friends at the forest’s edge. They decide to investigate. They listen closely, record the sound, and search for clues. They notice the noise only happens when the wind blows a certain way. They spot broken branches and, finally, catch a glimpse of a bird making that exact same call. Mystery solved—not by guessing, but by hunting for evidence and putting ideas to the test.
This way of thinking doesn’t always come easy. It’s natural to want to believe what’s comfortable or familiar. But science is built on the idea that anyone—wherever they are—can check the evidence themselves. If something is true, it should be true no matter who’s looking.
Sometimes, this process can be slow and, honestly, pretty frustrating. Imagine a scientist who spends years studying a rare plant, only to realize that an early experiment was off. Meanwhile, across the globe, another researcher tries the same experiment and gets a different result. Instead of quitting, they share what they’ve learned, compare notes, and try again. Little by little, mistakes get ironed out, and things start to make more sense.
That’s what sets science apart from myth. Myths are powerful stories, but they don’t bend when new evidence shows up. Science, on the other hand, is always willing to update. If a better explanation comes along, the old one steps aside. That doesn’t mean science is wishy-washy or unreliable—far from it. It means science is always working its way closer to the truth, one careful test at a time.
And here’s something most people don’t even notice: so much of everyday life depends on this way of thinking. The medicine that heals you, the technology that keeps you connected, even your understanding of how the world works—all of it comes from asking good questions, testing ideas, and trusting real evidence over old habits. It’s not always easy, but it’s the best tool we’ve got for figuring out what’s really true.
